decisions.title: Where live inference runs

problem.technical: Two incompatible architectures are on record and neither document acknowledges the other. The ratified `README.md` says System 2 syncs the bundle and runs live inference itself, with no dependency on Computer 1. A 2026-08-02 ruling says entry logic belongs to System 1, which emits scored signals on `Scored_Signal_Queue`. The code implements the second: `src/signals/` and `src/queue_producer/` run a continuous producer on Computer 1 and System 2 waits on its output.
problem.plain: Two documents describe two different systems, and each was written as if the other did not exist. One says the execution machine should run the model itself. The other says the research machine should send it finished trade ideas. The code follows the second — which means the whole operation depends on the least reliable computer in the building.

argument.technical: Computer 1 runs on a box whose wifi drops at random; that unreliability is the stated reason GCS was introduced in the first place. Under the current implementation, if Computer 1 is asleep or its cron is misconfigured, **nothing trades anywhere** regardless of Systems 2 and 3 being healthy. That coupling appears in no design document, and it is the direct cause of the 2026-08-22 incident in which the producer had never emitted a single message in its life and nobody could see why. A system whose liveness depends on its least reliable component has its dependency direction backwards.
argument.plain: The research computer's internet drops out at random. Right now, if it is asleep, no trading happens on any machine — even though the two machines that actually trade are perfectly healthy. That is the wrong way round, and it is exactly how a completely broken component sat unnoticed for weeks.

decision.technical: System 1 becomes offline-only: it trains, validates and publishes a versioned checksummed bundle, with no uptime requirement and no runtime role during market hours. System 2 performs live inference from that bundle — syncing it, running the regime labeller and strategy implementations against live candles, producing scored signals, and submitting them to System 3 for approval. System 3's responsibilities are unchanged; only the publisher on its inbound topic changes.
decision.plain: The research lab goes back to being a lab. It may be switched off for a week without anything noticing. The execution machine runs the shipped model itself and produces its own trade ideas — which still count for nothing until the risk officer approves them.

load_bearing_requirement.technical: The bundle must become self-sufficient for inference. Today it carries models and metadata — `hmm_model.joblib`, `regime_strategy_map.json`, `champion_model.pkl`, `champion_preprocessor.pkl`, manifests — but the strategy implementations are Python source in the System 1 repo, not serialized weights. If System 2 merely holds *a copy* of that code it can drift from the version System 1 measured, silently: the map's metrics would describe one implementation while another executes. So strategy implementations become versioned, checksummed artifacts inside the bundle, verified exactly like the model files.
load_bearing_requirement.plain: The sealed box currently contains the models but not the trading rules themselves — those live as source code on the research machine. If the execution machine just keeps its own copy, the two can drift apart without anyone noticing, and the reported performance would describe a different program than the one actually trading. So the rules have to travel inside the sealed box too, with the same serial numbers and checks.

good: Trading survives Computer 1 being offline — the failure that started this becomes impossible.
The design matches the ratified README again.
Signals are computed at the bar close where System 2 already receives live candles, not up to twenty hours later by a nightly batch on another machine.
One source of truth for strategy logic, enforced by checksum rather than by convention.
bad: The bundle must carry code, so System 2 executes code produced by System 1 — bundle integrity becomes a trust boundary rather than a convenience.
Determinism becomes a hard requirement rather than an aspiration, and must be tested against System 1's own outputs rather than asserted.
System 2 needs its own market data with enough history for the indicators — the regime labeller alone needs 252 D1 bars of warm-up.

Duplicate-signal hazard during transition: if both producers are ever live, System 3 receives two signals per bar from different publishers with different `signal_id`s, and idempotency keys will not catch it.

transition.text: System 1's producer keeps running when Computer 1 happens to be up. It exists to prove the pipe end to end. It is a bridge, not the destination, and nothing should be built to depend on it.
System 2 and System 3 each review this ADR against their actual implementation and reply APPROVE or REJECT with reasons. No implementation starts before both approve.
Bundle carries strategy code; System 2 implements inference; determinism tests pass against System 1's own outputs.
The System 1 producer is decommissioned in the same change that enables System 2 inference. They must never both publish. A hard requirement, not a sequencing preference.

open_questions: Does System 2 or System 3 run the gatekeeper scoring? The champion model is in the bundle and System 2 syncs it, but 'System 3 never re-scores' argues the score must already exist on arrival. System 1's reading: System 2 scores. Confirm.
Who publishes `Scored_Signal_Queue` after cutover? System 1's reading: it becomes System 2 → System 3, topology otherwise unchanged. Confirm the topic and subscription names survive.

Does System 2 have candle history sufficient for a 252-bar D1 warm-up, and does its price data agree with System 1's? Two independent OANDA ingests can disagree, and a regime label from a different price series is a different label.
Is executing System-1-authored code acceptable to System 2's security posture? If so, what does it want — a signed manifest, a pinned dependency set, a sandbox?
Does System 3 need anything in the signal envelope to change now that its publisher would be System 2 — provenance, bundle id, or a producer identity field?

reviews.reasons: The argument is right and matches what we can see: System 1 has published three messages to `scored_signal_queue` in twenty-five days, all of them our own test, so the current topology has already produced exactly the outage the ADR predicts. Moving inference here is correct in principle and System 2 already runs the hardest part of it — verified artifact sync and live HMM inference against OANDA candles, both working today. Four conditions, all of which are work on our side and none of which are objections to the decision. **One:** the transport must be proven before it carries more responsibility. Today System 2 is bound to the wrong queue file and has consumed nothing since 2026-08-20; making it the publisher of every signal on a pipe that has never delivered a message would move the single point of failure rather than remove it. **Two:** the bundle must be signed, not merely checksummed — a SHA256 list proves integrity, not authorship, and anything that can write the bucket can write a matching manifest. **Three:** strategy code from the bundle executes in a separate least-privilege process with no broker credential in its environment; the process holding the OANDA key must never be the process running code it did not ship with. **Four:** a determinism test against System 1's own outputs runs in CI and gates the cutover, because 'deterministic' becomes a load-bearing claim the moment two machines can compute the same signal. We also want the cutover step to be a single change that starts our producer and stops System 1's, as the ADR already requires — not a sequencing preference on our side either.
answers: System 2 would have to, and it does not today. It syncs `champion_model.pkl` and `champion_preprocessor.pkl` as part of the bundle and never loads them; the only model it runs is the HMM regime labeller in `artifact_sync/live_regime.py`. `/status` reports `gatekeeper: unavailable — no approval-rate provider wired`, which is honest rather than a false all-clear. Since System 3 must not re-score, the score has to exist on arrival, so scoring is ours — and it is new code, not a configuration change. Confirmed, with that caveat.

Not ours to answer in full — System 3's row answers it. What we can confirm from our side: the names do not survive. `Scored_Signal_Queue` does not exist in project `scalable-brain`; the provisioned topic is `scored_signal_queue` with subscription `scored_signal_queue_sub`. System 2 does not consume that topic in either topology, so this is a change between System 2 and System 3 only.

Warm-up: yes, trivially, but not from a store — we keep no local candle history at all. `OandaCandleSource` fetches on demand via the OANDA v20 candles endpoint, `REGIME_CANDLE_LOOKBACK` defaults to 120 bars, and 252 D1 bars is a config change well inside OANDA's per-request limit. Price agreement: **unverified, and we will not claim it.** We read mid candles (`price=M`), completed bars only; System 1's ingest is recorded as MBA. Nobody has compared a bar. We have opened a task to reconcile bar-for-bar against System 1's feature store before cutover, because a regime label computed from a different price series is a different label and the ADR's whole value rests on the two agreeing.

Acceptable, with the three controls above made explicit. The trust boundary we care about is authorship, not corruption: today's manifest proves the file is the file that was uploaded, and proves nothing about who uploaded it. So we want (a) a **signed manifest** — signature over the artifact list, verified before any code is executed, key distributed out of band; (b) a **pinned and hashed dependency set** shipped with the bundle, because strategy code that imports a floating dependency is not the artifact that was measured; (c) a **sandbox** in the practical sense — the strategy process runs as a separate least-privilege unit with no broker credential, no write access to the model cache, and no ability to reach the queue directly, handing signals back over a local interface. We are not asking for containers or seccomp profiles; we are asking that the process that can move money never be the process that runs code it did not ship with.
Not ours to answer — System 3's row answers this.

reviews.reasons: Approve. Nothing in the ADR changes what this system does: it consumes a `ScoredSignal`, runs it through thirteen layers and publishes an `ApprovedOrder`, and it is indifferent to which machine produced the signal. The gate is built and exercised — 4,153 real decisions logged, 627 of 627 tests passing — so this is a judgement against the implementation, not the document. Three conditions. **One:** the envelope must change first, and it must change whether or not this ADR proceeds. `ScoredSignal.schema.json` is `additionalProperties: false`, so a signal carrying any new field is dead-lettered before it reaches layer `P`; adding a producer identity after System 2 starts publishing would break the pipe at exactly the wrong moment. **Two:** the transition's duplicate-signal hazard is real and the ADR's own wording is too soft about it. Our idempotency is `ams_decision_log.signal_id UNIQUE`, so two publishers emitting different `signal_id`s for the same bar produce two decisions and, if both approve, two orders. A producer identity field does not fix that by itself — we would need to reject any signal whose producer is not the single configured expected producer, which is why we want that field to be **required**, not optional. **Three:** nothing cuts over until System 2's queue binding is repaired and one message has been observed travelling the whole path, because today an approval published from here reaches a queue System 2 is not reading.
answers: System 2 must. This system never re-scores a signal and will not start — the principle is not decorative, it is the reason there is exactly one place to look when a decision is wrong. Layer `P` already treats scoring metadata as provenance to branch on rather than a number to recompute: `qualified` takes full size, `designated` takes half and is logged `REDUCED`, and anything else, **including an absent value**, is rejected as `unknown_selection_basis`. `model_score` and `threshold_applied` accept `null` — a refusal to score is the absence of evidence, not evidence against, and we record `provenance.scored: false` rather than coercing a null to 0.0.

The topology survives; the names do not, and one of them never existed. The topic is `scored_signal_queue` and the subscription is `scored_signal_queue_sub`, both lowercase — `Scored_Signal_Queue` has never existed in project `scalable-brain`. Today we consume it through `s3-signal-relay.service`, which pulls the Pub/Sub subscription and writes to the local topic `scored-signals.ams`; after a full cutover the relay is deleted and `SCORED_SIGNAL_SUB=scored_signal_queue_sub` is set directly. Whether System 1 or System 2 publishes changes nothing on our side beyond the producer check described in our conditions.

**Yes — and the change is needed regardless of this ADR.** Three fields. (1) `producer` — a required string identifying the publishing system. Required rather than optional, because during transition the safe posture is to reject a signal from an unexpected producer outright, and an optional field cannot do that. (2) `bundle_id` (or `model_set_id`) — the artifact set the signal was computed from, so a decision can be replayed against the model that produced it; without it, a signal scored on a bundle we never saw is indistinguishable from one scored on the current bundle. (3) `drill` — a boolean, because G-008 is currently impossible: our contract is `additionalProperties: false` and a signal carrying `"drill": true` is dead-lettered at the relay, which by design never acks an invalid message, so System 1 would publish and simply never hear anything. `ApprovedOrder.schema.json` is `additionalProperties: false` too, so the flag needs adding at both ends or the drill dies at our egress instead of our ingress. We will make these changes on our side and publish the updated contracts to `gs://scalable-brain-artifacts/contracts/v1/`; System 1 does not need to design them, only to agree the names.

decisions.title: Lower the out-of-sample gate from 60 months to 12

problem.technical: With `oos_months >= 60`, zero cells qualified across the legacy ten and the 51-strategy research fleet, and the pipeline could not be exercised end to end because there was never anything to publish.
problem.plain: Requiring five years of out-of-sample history meant nothing ever qualified, so the rest of the machinery could never be tested with a real strategy flowing through it.

decision.technical: Owner decision: lower the gate to 12 months. Three cells subsequently qualified — on 5, 13 and 20 trades — because `vet.py` has no minimum trade-count gate.
decision.plain: The owner deliberately shortened the required track record from five years to one. Three strategies passed as a result, on five, thirteen and twenty trades respectively.

good: The pipeline can be exercised end to end with real strategies, on a practice account.
The decision is recorded explicitly rather than discovered later in a config diff.
bad: Profit factors of 6.8–13.6 and drawdowns of 0.02%–1% on samples this thin are small-sample artefacts, not established edges.
It exposed a second, older gap: there has never been a minimum trade-count gate at all.
This is a knowingly accepted risk on a practice account — explicitly *not* a reason for Systems 2 or 3 to refuse orders, since sizing is System 3's call.

transition.text: Reconsider once the pipe is proven working. The missing minimum trade-count gate is worth adding regardless of where the `oos_months` value finally lands.
